question: An animated background band is stored in a slot whose size was fixed back when no act had one, and a real band needs about four thousand times that. Fixing the slot is easy; the question is how big to make it. A band's size depends entirely on how big an author draws it, and the legal range runs from 302 bytes to about 112 KB - a 380x spread. Whatever we pick, an author who draws a bigger band than that gets a build failure, so this is really a question about how much background animation you want to be possible without an engine change.

options.name: Pick a generous ceiling now and refuse politely above it
options.what: We reserve room for a band up to 16 tiles wide by 8 tall - about eight times the one Aurora just drew, and comfortably inside the spare room that already exists next to it. Anything bigger stops the build with a message naming the limit, instead of the cryptic collision we get today. Authors never think about this again until they hit the ceiling.
options.costs: About 32 KB of cartridge space set aside whether or not an act uses it. You have roughly 350 KB spare, so it is not tight. If you ever want a band bigger than that, raising it is a small change but it is a change.

options.name: Reserve enough for the biggest band that could ever exist
options.what: Room for a band covering every tile the background has. No author can ever hit a limit, and this question never comes back.
options.costs: About 112 KB set aside permanently, which is very nearly all the spare room in that part of the cartridge. It would leave that neighbourhood with almost nothing left for anything else later.

options.name: Re-measure the layout every time the band changes size
options.what: No space is wasted and no ceiling exists. The layout is recomputed to fit whatever the author actually drew.
options.costs: Every time you resize a band, the cartridge layout has to be re-measured and re-approved in the assembler's repo - a deliberate act in a different project. It turns a normal art tweak into a cross-project chore, which cuts against the whole point of the effects work: that something you build in the editor just reaches the game.

recommend.because: It is the only option that costs you nothing at authoring time and does not spend the room you may want later. It also matches how this engine already handles the same kind of limit elsewhere - the number of bands is a declared ceiling with a guard that names it - so it is the consistent choice rather than a new idea. And the failure it produces is a sentence telling an author their band is too big, which is the failure you want if you are ever going to hit one.

Art_Sonic is ~97,469 B, consistent with this engine's uncompressed sprite art. detail: THE PREMISE OF d-9/d-10 WAS WRONG AND THIS IS THE THIRD CORRECTION ON THIS QUESTION - but unlike the first two it came from measurement, not from me re-reading a table. question: For a long act where the background changes as you travel, forest giving way to cave, the background is stored in fixed height chunks. How tall should one chunk be? The hardware scroll plane is 512 pixels tall, so a chunk that size wraps for free. Half that size fits twice as many different backgrounds into the same vertical space, but the engine then has to track the top and bottom halves of the plane separately.

options.name: Full height chunks, 512 pixels
options.what: The wrap logic is trivial and hard to get wrong. Each chunk is a generous amount of vertical space for one look.
options.costs: Fewer distinct backgrounds per act. If you want a look that changes every screen or two vertically, this will feel coarse.

options.name: Half height chunks, 256 pixels
options.what: Twice as many background looks in the same act, so vertical travel can change scenery much more often.
options.costs: The engine tracks two halves of the scroll plane independently, which is the part of this system most likely to produce a seam glitch. Adds engine work to a system that is not built yet.

recommend.because: This system is unbuilt, so the first version should be the one that is hard to get wrong. Vertical scenery changes every 512 pixels is already far more than the current level uses, and if an act ever genuinely needs finer grain, halving the chunk later is a change inside this subsystem rather than a redesign.

question: How the music driver stores pitch. Today each note is a raw chip frequency number. The alternative is to store a musical value instead and work out the chip number from it. The study that surveyed other Genesis drivers calls this the single biggest musical correctness idea it found: pitch bends, vibrato and detune would behave the same way in every octave instead of drifting as notes get higher. It changes the format every song is saved in, so it wants to happen before there is much music, and it is a big enough bet that it should be your call rather than mine.

options.name: Change it now, before the soundtrack grows
options.what: Every song written from here on gets correct bends and vibrato across the whole keyboard. The one existing test track gets converted.
options.costs: A sound driver work package plus a matching change in the music tool, and the two have to land together. Roughly a week across both.

options.name: Do it after the currently planned sound work
options.what: The banked driver packages land first in the order already planned.
options.costs: Any music written in the meantime is in the old format and has to be converted later, and conversion is exactly the step where songs get subtly wrong.

options.name: Leave pitch as raw chip numbers
options.what: No work, and the driver stays simpler.
options.costs: Bends and vibrato stay octave dependent forever. It is the kind of flaw a listener will not name but will hear as the music sounding slightly cheap in the high registers.

recommend.because: The cost of this change is almost entirely proportional to how much music already exists, and right now that is nearly none. Every week it waits it gets more expensive and more likely to be skipped for good. There is also a second improvement, a shared pitch envelope, that is only worth doing alongside this one, so answering this settles two things.

question: A hardware limitation, and it needs a choice rather than a fix. question: We found why the background effect does not show, and it is an engine bug rather than anything about the effect. The hardware can be told to change the horizontal scroll either once per screen line or once per eight-line row. The once-per-eight-rows path has been written wrong since it was added, and it has never run in any build until now, because your showcase scene is the first thing that ever asked for it. It fills only the top four rows of the screen and leaves the rest reading memory nothing wrote, which is exactly the frozen foreground and the two moving bands at the top that you saw. Fixing it is not the question. The question is which way, because the cheap path turns out not to be cheap.

options.name: Delete the eight-row path, always scroll per line
options.what: One code path instead of two, and the whole class of bug goes away. Everything in the game today already uses the per line path, so nothing on screen changes anywhere.
options.costs: The engine always sends the full scroll table to the hardware, about 896 bytes a frame, which is what it already does everywhere today. You give up a saving that was never real.

options.name: Fix the eight-row path and keep it
options.what: Both paths work. The eight-row one still saves the processor some work building the table, about a quarter of the effort.
options.costs: It has to send the same 896 bytes to the hardware as the per line path, so the saving is only in processor time and not in transfer. Two code paths to keep correct, and this one just proved it can sit broken for months without anyone noticing.

options.name: Fix it, and add a build time check that the two halves agree
options.what: Same as fixing it, plus the build refuses when a scene asks for one mode while the engine picks the other. That disagreement is a real second bug we found alongside this one.
options.costs: A bit more work now. It is the only option that stops the same family of bug reaching you again through a different door.

recommend.because: The separate bug we found is that three different pieces of the engine decide independently whether a scene is per line or per eight rows, and they can disagree. One of them is already disagreeing on the current build, harmlessly, by luck. That is how this reached you: nothing was watching. Fixing the fill without adding the check leaves the door open. If you would rather not carry two paths at all, deleting is a perfectly good answer and I would not argue hard, since the saving it protects is processor time only.

detail: ROOT CAUSE, verified firsthand. Parallax_Fill_PerCell (engine/level/parallax.emp) packs 28 cell entries CONSECUTIVELY via `move.l d0,(a4)+`, stride 4, and Enqueue_Dirty_Buffers (engine/system/buffers.emp:156) ships dma_length(112). The VDP in cell mode indexes the HScroll table at byte offset (line & ~7)*4, i.e. stride 32 per cell row, so 112 bytes feed cell rows 0-3 only and screen lines 32-223 read VRAM never written (measured zero, 196 of 196 entries). Plane A's word is zero too, which is why the FOREGROUND freezes. Never fired before: master f8d06cae has 21 parallax configs, all per-line, ZERO per-cell; the branch adds exactly one, EditorSceneBinding_OJZ_Act1_Sec4. Single-variable proof: flipping one token in parallax_mode_key (bne .mode_per_line -> jbra), FAST DEBUG e2d3b102, nothing else, makes the frozen region scroll AND makes the curve appear. SECOND DEFECT (the guard option): three keys decide per-line vs per-cell independently - scene_forces_per_line() sees curve/precision/off-grid tops, parallax_mode_key() sees only header deform tables and the anchor and picks BOTH the fill and the DMA length, and the reg $0B derivation sees only the deform tables. parallax_config has no precision field, so a curve scene cannot request per-line at runtime. scene() already guards this exact shape for deform: Own(..) and has no guard for the other three arms. tools/curve_probe.py's docstring asserts this cannot happen and is wrong.

question: You asked me to double check the scroll table finding and pick the direction. The finding holds: I re-read the code and re-ran the scan myself, and every load bearing claim checks out (the fill packs its entries four bytes apart where the hardware reads them thirty two apart; the transfer is 112 bytes; all 21 configs in the shipped game take the per line path; and there really are three separate places deciding the mode, one of which already disagrees on the current build at the very first section you play). What I have to correct is the menu you were given. Option 'fix' would NOT make your curve appear: a curve lives only in the per line fill, and the scene has no way to ask for per line at run time, so a repaired eight row path would scroll correctly and still draw no curve. And option 'fix with a check' as written would make the build REFUSE your showcase scene, because the check would catch exactly this scene disagreeing with itself. So the real choice is between deleting the eight row path or fixing it AND giving it one shared switch.

options.name: Delete the eight row path. One way to scroll, always per line.
options.what: Your curve appears with no further design work. The whole family of bug is gone by construction: no switch, no three places to disagree, the hardware register set once. The 21 shipped configs already take this path so nothing you can see changes anywhere else. The 'precision' setting in the editor goes away too; it never changed any picture, because no scene ever ran the other way.
options.costs: You give up about 400 processor cycles a frame on scenes with nothing fancy in them, a third of one percent of a frame. The starter 'demo' game currently relies on the eight row path as its only one, so it grows by a few hundred bytes (to be measured, not booked). A wider cleanup: several build time checks, cost model rows and the editor's schema field all exist only because of the eight row path and get retired with it. This is a byte moving change to both games.

options.name: Fix the eight row path, and make ONE byte in the config decide the mode for everyone
options.what: The eight row fill writes its entries where the hardware reads them. A spare reserved byte in the config header (there is one, so records do not grow) is set at build time by the same rule that already decides per line, and the fill, the transfer length and the hardware register all read that one byte. Your curve appears because the build marks the scene per line. The editor keeps its 'precision' setting.
options.costs: Two fill routines stay alive, and one of them still has no user in the game. The only thing it buys is those 400 cycles a frame. It needs a gate that actually watches the eight row path render during motion, which is the thing nobody had, or it can rot again unnoticed. Also byte moving.

options.name: Fix the eight row fill only (the option you were offered an hour ago)
options.what: The frozen foreground is repaired.
options.costs: Your curve still does not draw. The three way disagreement stays. Not a real option; listed so you can see why it dropped off.

recommend.because: The eight row path has had zero users since it was written, was broken from birth, and its entire benefit is a third of a percent of a frame. Everything built around it (five build time rules, a run time switch, a hardware register toggle, an editor field, cost model rows) exists to manage a limitation nobody is using. Your standing rule for this engine is delete old paths rather than carry dormant ones, and this is the cleanest instance of it I have seen. The one number that could change my mind is how much the starter demo grows; the parcel measures that first and reports before it lands. If it is more than you want to pay in the lean shape, fix-single-key is the fallback and I would take it without complaint.

question: You asked whether the original games actually limit fall speed. They do not: I read both reference games' air movement and neither caps how fast the player falls; gravity just keeps adding. Dropping the limit to 15 closes the gap and is a one number change. options.what: The fall through hole is gone, in every level, permanently.
options.costs: Falling at terminal speed is about six percent slower than it is today, near the edge of noticeable. The recorded regression tests have to be re-recorded because they track the player frame by frame.

options.name: Keep 16 and live with the hole
options.what: Nothing changes; the limit stays where we first set it.
options.costs: A known way to fall through a floor stays in the shipped game. It needs a thin floor and terminal speed together, so it is rare, and rare bugs are the ones that show up in front of an audience. (It no longer buys fidelity: the originals have no limit at all.)

options.name: Fix it properly with finer collision stepping
options.what: The hole closes and the fall speed is untouched.
options.costs: Much more expensive, and it touches the collision path that everything else depends on. Weeks, not minutes.

options.name: No fall limit; camera capped; collision follows Sonic
options.what: Falls feel exactly like the originals. Sonic can outrun the camera in a long fall and drift down the screen, which is what the originals do too.

Second, and this is the part the idea does not remove: at 32 pixels a frame the sensor can skip any floor thinner than 32, so the finer collision stepping from the expensive option becomes mandatory rather than optional. Weeks, and it touches the streaming and collision paths everything else depends on.

recommend.because: Still the one-constant fix for the shipped hole. The uncapped shape is the faithful long road and it is worth keeping on the card, but it is the expensive option plus a streaming parcel, not an alternative to it.

detail: Measured 2026-08-26 on the running ROM. Engine: bg_scroll = ((camY - v_center_y) >> v_factor_bg) + v_offset, written signed to VSRAM; Plane B is 512 px so the VDP takes it mod 512. Witnessed: camY 61 -> scroll -57 -> VDP row 455; predicted seam 57 px down and confirmed by a background-only capture. Hand-recompute ((61-512)>>3)+0 = -57 matches the engine's stored value. question: Loops need a way for the level to say 'here is where the player crosses from the upper track to the lower one'. You chose painting that into the level rather than placing markers. We just found that the painted information has nowhere to go: the build step boils each cell down to an index that describes only its SHAPE, its ANGLE and its SOLIDITY - so two cells that differ only in a crossing point come out identical. This needs a change to how level data is stored, which is why it is yours. Which way?

options.name: Add the crossing to what makes a cell unique (RECOMMENDED)
options.what: The index that already describes each cell grows to include the crossing. Costs no extra memory in the game and nothing extra to look up while playing, because the engine already fetches that index for every step the player takes.
options.costs: The table of distinct cell types grows - two cells with identical geometry but different crossings become two entries. We use 21 of 256 today, so there is room, but I cannot tell you the exact growth until we know how many distinct crossing kinds a loop needs. It also mixes 'what this ground looks like' with 'where the path switches', which are different ideas sharing one number.

options.name: Store the crossings separately
options.what: A second layer of data alongside the collision, holding only crossings. Keeps the two ideas cleanly apart, and the crossing can be as detailed as we like without touching the shape table.
options.costs: Real memory: roughly one byte per cell across every section of every act, whether or not it has a loop in it. That is the largest cost of the three and it is paid by levels that never use the feature.

options.name: Store only the cells that HAVE a crossing
options.what: A short list per section rather than a value on every cell. Almost no memory, since a level has a handful of crossings and thousands of cells.
options.costs: The engine has to search that list as the player moves, which is work on the most performance-sensitive path in the game - the ground check that runs several times per frame. It is the cheapest in memory and the most likely to cost speed.

recommend.because: It is the only one of the three that costs nothing while the game is running - the engine already reads that index for every ground check, so the crossing arrives free. The memory cost is zero and the table has room. Its real drawback is conceptual rather than practical: it ties a cell's identity to its crossing, so the same piece of ground painted with and without one becomes two entries. I would rather pay that than pay memory on every level that has no loop, or pay speed on the hottest code in the engine.

question: You asked whether we are limited to 512 pixels of height when S3K zones run to about 2600. Short answer: no, and the limit is not where it looks. Your LEVELS are not capped at 512 - OJZ act 1 is already 6144 pixels tall, more than twice the tallest S3K zone, and the foreground handles that by streaming tiles down and up exactly the way it already streams them left and right. The 512 belongs to the BACKGROUND IMAGE: the background is painted into the video chip's plane once and then only scrolled, and that plane is 512 pixels tall. So the real question is what a background does in an act taller than the plane can hold.

options.name: Keep the background scrolling at half rate (what is in now)
options.what: The background moves 1/16 per pixel of camera instead of 1/8, so the 512-pixel image covers acts up to 8192 pixels tall without ever wrapping. Nothing to build, nothing to draw.
options.costs: The background moves half as much when you go up and down, so the scene reads as flatter. It is a look cost, not a technical one, and it is the only cost.

options.name: Redraw the art so its top joins its bottom
options.what: If the image tiles seamlessly top to bottom, wrapping stops being visible and the background can scroll at the original rate with no height limit at all.
options.costs: An art job on every background that needs it, and it constrains what those backgrounds can depict - a horizon cannot tile.

options.name: Let a background be taller than the plane
options.what: Stream background rows the way the foreground already streams them, so a background can be any height and scroll at any rate.
options.costs: This is engineering rather than a choice you can price today. It is not a new mechanism - the foreground's row streaming already exists and would be extended to the second plane - but the background stops being one picture and becomes a tall map, which changes how you author it and how it interacts with the animated colour bands. I would want to scope and price it before you commit to it.

recommend.because: For anything S3K-sized this question does not arise at all: at the original scroll rate a 512-pixel background already covers acts up to 4096 pixels, and S3K's tallest zone is around 2600. The pressure comes from OUR act being 6144, which is taller than anything S3K shipped. The half-rate setting covers up to 8192 and costs only depth of feel, so it is the right thing to run on while we decide - and if a specific scene looks flat because of it, that is the moment to spend the art or the engineering, on that scene, with a reason.

question: You asked about background ART taller than the plane, and whether Sky Sanctuary's is about 2,600 pixels. You are right - it is 2,816 pixels tall, about 2,530 of it scrolled through in one continuous run. But the mechanism is the reverse of what it sounds like, and it makes this much cheaper than either of us assumed. S3K's scroll planes are HALF the height of ours: 512x256 where ours are 512x512. S3K got a 2,816-pixel background out of a 256-pixel window by streaming rows in as you move, which is a genuinely tall map and not a trick. Our plane already holds twice S3K's entire window. And Sky Sanctuary needed 2,816 only because its background moves 1:1 with the level, with no depth division at all. Our OJZ background at its current depth would need 740 pixels. So the question is whether to spend a small parcel buying that, against a plane that is already twice the size S3K managed with.

options.name: Build it - backgrounds stream rows like the foreground already does
options.what: Backgrounds stop being capped by the plane. Any height, any depth. You could author a Sky Sanctuary-class background, and the current half-rate scroll becomes something you can take back.
options.costs: One routine and a scheduler in the engine - about 350 bytes, 4 bytes of memory, no new video memory, and 33 bytes a frame of transfer, which is half a percent of the budget. It is 8 times cheaper than the foreground's version because the background moves 8 times slower. The real cost is on the art side: a background becomes a 512x744 image instead of 512x512, the editor's canvas becomes a strip with a viewport, and its live preview needs rebuilding because it currently assumes the background never redraws. One more thing to know: it does NOT lift the 448-tile ceiling, and it makes that ceiling bite about 45 percent harder, because the same tiles now have to cover more area.

options.name: Stay at half-rate scroll (what is in now)
options.what: Nothing to build. The 512-pixel background covers acts up to 8,192 pixels tall.
options.costs: The background moves half as much vertically, so scenes read flatter. Nothing forecloses the build later - the two do not conflict.

options.name: Redraw the art to join top-to-bottom
options.what: If the image tiles seamlessly, wrapping stops being visible and the original scroll rate comes back.
options.costs: An art job per background, and it constrains what they can depict - a horizon cannot tile.

recommend.because: Because it turned out small. The engine half is one parcel against machinery that already exists for the foreground, and the numbers are not close to any ceiling. What makes it worth ruling on rather than just doing is the art and editor half, which is the bigger item and is yours: a background becomes a tall strip to draw, and the editor needs work to author and preview one. My suggested order is to keep the half-rate scroll shipping now - it costs nothing and is zero-risk - and take the engine parcel when you want a background that actually needs the height, so the art pass happens for a scene you care about rather than speculatively.

The only hardware-TESTED rule (Eke) is that an H40 partial column renders at VSRAM[$4C] & VSRAM[$4E], the same value for both planes; oracle implements exactly that and so does Genesis Plus GX ('verified on PAL MD2'). options.what: You describe it in whatever words you like: roughly where on screen (top, bottom, the whole column, how wide), when it happens (act start, after running right a while, after a warp, when you look up, when you come back left), and whether it ever fills back in. I start the hunt from that instead of from the source.
options.costs: A couple of minutes of your time, and you may have to go and reproduce it once to be sure.

options.name: I hunt it blind
options.what: I take the mechanism families nothing has looked at yet - the vertical axis, art-pool page eviction, the background and parallax path, palette, BgAnim - and sweep them with agents.
options.costs: Real time and tokens across several agents, with a decent chance of a third confident wrong answer. Everything examined so far has been the horizontal streaming path because that is where the first guess pointed.

options.name: Make the ROM catch it for us
options.what: I build a debug capture that records the moment a column is drawn blank - what the cache thought, what the camera was doing, which frame. Next time you see it, the ROM tells us what happened instead of us guessing.
options.costs: A parcel of engine work before it can catch anything, and it only pays off the next time the bug shows up. It is also the option that survives if the bug turns out to be rare or input-dependent.

recommend.because: It is free and it is the only option that changes the odds. Both dead suspects came from reading code and picking the mechanism that looked wrong; that has now failed twice in a row on the same bug. One sentence from you about where on screen it happens would cut the search space more than another full night of derivation, and it costs you less than either alternative. If your answer turns out not to narrow it, the capture option is still there and would be better aimed for having heard it.

detail: Two suspects dead. (1) Partial fill: killed by Cache_Fill_Resume_Col reading $FFFF at all 150 settled samples; the fix that came out of it (839d600d, merged 42cb5781) is a real bug and its own subject says it does not fix the reported hole. (2) The 64-vs-80 head-column over-claim: REFUTED and landed at 0ea56d94. The over-claim is real - Tile_Cache_Init seeds Cache_Head_Col at Left+79 while Section_RedrawPlanes' .pla_fill walks 64 columns - but Section_UpdateColumns' .left_done cross-clamp (section.emp:664-666) writes Right = min(Right, Left_Col_Written + 63) and the left loop targets exactly cam_col, so the tracker collapses to the drawn extent on the first frame that runs the streaming loops. OJZ act 1 starts at Camera_X 96 (cam_col 12), four columns to drain, one frame, camera at rest. Verified firsthand by the overseer before landing on four joints, by a different route than the agent: the Section_Plane_Dirty writer population (exactly two, both in ojz_scroll_test.emp, plus one clr.b), the cross-clamp's branch direction, the 80/20 and 0..63 constants, and the act descriptor's start coords. The agent contradicted its brief on the threshold and was right: the over-claim needs cam_col < 16, not < 20; that wrong number came from the booking via the overseer's brief. Residual latent defect booked separately: section.emp:462 assigns Cache_Head_Col unconditionally under a comment reading 'clamp to cache range', while the d5 half three lines above is a real max. Zero observable delta today; goes live the moment a third Section_Plane_Dirty setter appears, and the header at :168 already advertises a cache-recovery path that does not exist yet. Queued as its own byte-moving parcel. An emulator confirmation of the refutation is queued but deliberately not yet run: read Section_Right_Col_Written one frame after GameState_OJZScroll_Init returns; 75 confirms, 79 would reopen it. Held so it runs in the same emulator session as the sighting-driven hunt rather than spending a boot on confirming a negative.

question: Sonic's heaviest animation frames need more art transfers than the queue has room for. The instrument to see it is built and about to land. Fixing the underlying overrun is a separate call, and it changes shipped art data - which of the three ways do you want?

options.name: Re-cut only the six worst frames (recommended)
options.what: Six of Sonic's frames need more than the safe limit. Appending 112 tiles of art and rewriting just those six drops the worst frame from thirteen transfers to ten, which is exactly the safe number - so the real build-time check switches on and the temporary one retires. Costs about 3.5 KB of ROM and needs a small new tool.
options.costs: 3,460 bytes of ROM, with about 20 KB of room to spare, so no other budget moves. A new tool to write, though most of it already exists. One risk I have NOT measured: appending art should disturb nothing else, and that is an argument rather than a measurement.

options.name: Re-cut all of Sonic's art
options.what: The thorough version. Drops the worst frame from thirteen transfers to two, the best possible result, and the tool for it already exists.
options.costs: 24,020 bytes of ROM against 24,160 available - it does NOT fit. It forces the sound banks to move and crushes the background-animation ceiling you already have a ruling on. Effectively this means paying for a ROM re-layout to buy headroom you do not need.

options.name: Just give the queue more room
options.what: Raise the queue from twelve slots to fifteen. Smallest possible change.
options.costs: Only 42 bytes of RAM, so RAM is not the objection. The objections are that a thirteen-transfer frame still costs thirteen transfers - the work does not go away, it just stops being refused - it shifts every RAM address after the queue, and fifteen leaves exactly the minimum reserve, which the code's own comment calls the floor rather than a comfortable margin. It hides a fixable data shape rather than fixing it.

recommend.because: It is the only option that ends with the build itself enforcing the limit, which means this cannot come back. It costs one seventh of the thorough option and fits without moving anything else you have already ruled on. The just-add-slots option is cheap in RAM and buys the least: the transfers still happen, so the frame is still the heaviest thing in the frame, and the next person to add a per-frame art producer walks into the same wall with the margin already spent. Worth knowing before you choose: this is not currently breaking your game in a way you have reported. The visible cost is background art loading stalling for a frame when the queue fills, which happens on two of Sonic's frames - looking up, and the second walk-tilt frame that occurs during ordinary running on slopes. The second one is the one that matters, because it burns the queue while the level is streaming.

detail: MY OWN BOOKING WAS WRONG AND AN AGENT REFUTED IT FROM SOURCE, verified firsthand here before writing this card. The booking said the guard 'is COMMENTED OUT at dplc.emp:76'. It is not: that line is a worked example with placeholder subject `_dplc_x` inside the doc comment for `dplc_peak_entries`, in a module that embeds no DPLC table. Five live ensures exist and were read here: knuckles_data.emp:148, tails_data.emp:83 (sums body + appendage), dust_data.emp:30, player_instashield.emp:476 (vs DMA_DEFERRABLE_SLOTS), and collision_data.emp:75 - the last being a deliberate ratchet at <=13 for Sonic carrying a written debt note that already names the re-page as the fix. So the budget was guarded and the overrun was recorded, not undetected. Second correction, also the agent's and also from source: the worst reachable frame is not only $C4 (LookUp). collision_data.emp records TWO frames at 12 - $C4 and $0E, the second walk-tilt frame, made selectable during ordinary running by Player_ApplyTilt. $0E is the one that matters because it burns the queue while streaming. Measured peaks, reproduced by a parser written fresh from the format spec: sonic 13 (frames $C1, $C8), knuckles 5, tails 2, tails_tail 1, dust 1, insta_shield 2 (Deferrable). Unoptimized sonic is 16. 13 + DPLC_ENTRY_RESERVE(2) > DMA_IMPORTANT_SLOTS(12), so the real ensure stays off until this is fixed. Option C mechanism: six frames exceed the real wall of 10 - $0E (12 entries), $BE (11), $BF (11), $C1 (13), $C4 (12), $C8 (13). Append 112 tiles, rewrite those six only: +3,584 B art, -124 B DPLC, net +3,460 B; entries collapse 72 -> 10; peak becomes exactly DMA_IMPORTANT_SLOTS - DPLC_ENTRY_RESERVE. Option B uses the existing tools/dplc_layout.py, peak 13 -> 2, but +24,020 B against a bganim_room report of 24,160 B release / 21,920 B DEBUG. NOTE a discrepancy I have not resolved: those room figures differ slightly from the 24,256 / 22,000 the hub is quoting on the EFFECTS-W1 blocker. Likely different tree states; do not build a decision on either number without re-deriving it. The instrument half is separate from this card and lands regardless: split counters (DMA_Split_Reject_Count for .split_reject, DMA_Overflow_Count kept for .full) plus all three DMA_Peak_* written for the first time, sampled in VInt_Level. Release ROM claimed md5-identical; to be re-verified on the merged tree with a current assembler, since the shared sigil binary is 19 crate-commits stale and the agent's CRCs were taken with a binary 18 commits behind sigil HEAD.

question: REPLACES d-47, because two of its numbers were wrong in a way that changes the shape of the choice. Sonic's heaviest frames need more art transfers than the queue has room for. Which fix do you want - and separately, do you want the ROM saving a peer study just found?

options.name: Re-cut only the six worst frames (still my recommendation)
options.what: Appending 112 tiles of art and rewriting six frames drops the worst frame from thirteen transfers to ten, which is exactly the safe number - so the build-time check switches on permanently and the temporary one retires. Costs 3,460 bytes and fits today with room to spare.
options.costs: A small new tool, most of which already exists. One risk I have still NOT measured: appending art should disturb nothing else, and that remains an argument rather than a measurement.

options.name: Free up ROM first, then re-cut everything
options.what: A peer study found we store the same level block data over and over - 443 stored copies of 73 distinct blocks. Removing the duplication frees about 21 KB with no new bookkeeping, and that space is in exactly the budget this competes for. With it freed, the thorough re-cut becomes affordable and drops the worst frame from thirteen transfers to two.
options.costs: Two parcels in a required order - the dedup MUST land first, because the thorough re-cut on today's tree physically overruns the sound-bank boundary by 2,100 bytes. Afterwards it fits with only 2,502 bytes of margin, about ten percent, thin enough that a stale measurement could eat it.

options.name: Just give the queue more room
options.what: Raise the queue from twelve slots to fifteen. Smallest change, 42 bytes of RAM.
options.costs: Unchanged from d-47 and still the weakest: the transfers still happen, it shifts every RAM address after the queue, and it spends the safety margin down to the floor rather than fixing the data.

options.name: Take the ROM saving on its own, decide the art fix later
options.what: Do the deduplication because 21 KB for no behaviour change is worth having regardless, and leave the transfer overrun where it is for now.
options.costs: The overrun stays. It is not currently breaking anything you have reported, but the build cannot enforce the limit until one of the art fixes lands.

recommend.because: Take the targeted re-cut, and take the deduplication too - but as two separate wins rather than as one sequence. The dedup is worth about 21 KB for no behaviour change and no new bookkeeping, which is worth having whatever you decide here. But making the thorough re-cut DEPEND on it buys you headroom you have no use for: it takes the worst frame to two transfers where ten is already safe, and it pays for that with a required ordering between two parcels and a ten percent margin afterwards. The targeted fix reaches the same decisive place - the build itself enforcing the limit, so this cannot come back - and it fits today with about 20 KB spare and no dependency on anything.

detail: TWO CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN d-47, both verified firsthand here. (1) I said option B needs 24,020 B against ~24,160 B available, i.e. narrowly doesn't fit. The real constraint is tighter and I had misread the instrument. tools/bganim_room.py's rom_room() returns anchor minus packed-data end - RAW bytes - and DATA_GROWTH_RESERVE (0x4000 = 16,384) is a separate floor the placement rule enforces, never included in that figure. Binding shape is DEBUG: room 21,920 B, so spendable is 21,920 - 16,384 = 5,536 B. Option B misses the gate by 18,484 B and PHYSICALLY overruns the dac_banks anchor by 2,100 B on today's tree. Re-derived independently by the overseer, not taken from the agent. (2) The block-stream saving makes it affordable, and it is in the SAME region - verified, not assumed: block blobs sit upstream of Art_Sonic in map.toml's order, inside the run dac_banks bounds. After dedup: 21,920 + 20,986 - 24,020 = 18,886, which is 2,502 B above the reserve. Fits, no anchor move, ruled 12,288 B BG-anim ceiling untouched. The study's own figures were wrong in its favour and its conclusion survived: 491 streams / 74 distinct is really 443 ROM-reaching entries / 73 distinct = 11,280 B, and the saving is 20,986 B not ~31 KB. Their 66% cross-dictionary duplication died to a control - the same 4-byte measure inside ONE dictionary gives 61.2%, so it was measuring its own method; real cross-dictionary redundancy is 66 B of 6,144 (1.1%). Act-wide dedup with one shared dictionary is 930 B WORSE than within-section sharing. CAVEAT THAT IS NOT DECORATIVE: 2,502 B is ten percent of option B's cost, and the release-shape room figure does not reproduce across sources (three different values seen: 24,160, 24,256, 24,464). DEBUG is the binding shape and it reproduces exactly, so the decision does not turn on it - but re-derive both numbers from a fresh build of both canonical shapes before committing to the dedup-then-full path. Unchanged from d-47: the guard was never commented out - that was my error, refuted from source; the overrun is a documented ratchet; two frames sit at the limit, $C4 (LookUp) and $0E (the second walk-tilt frame, reached during ordinary running on slopes), and $0E is the one that matters because it burns the queue while the level is streaming.
